summary:
The Human Margin is a five-chapter, choice-based survival game set at a lunar outpost on the rim of Shackleton Crater. Players manage Power, Air, Shield, Food, and a rover battery for a four-person crew, and every button shows its cost. The numbers that can kill you come from real NASA open data: DONKI space-weather records (archived May 2024 and September 2017 storms, plus a live 7-day flare check in the final chapter), OSDR Veggie plant experiments, LRO measurements of Shackleton’s size, lighting, and temperature, and NASA OCHMO limits for radiation (250 mSv per storm, 600 mSv career) and CO2 (3 mmHg).

Each risky choice echoes a real spaceflight mistake, from Apollo 12 to Apollo 13, Gemini 8, Skylab 4, and Mir. Failure leads to gentle “Learning Endings” with no graphic content, and a Data Journal links players to the real datasets.

The game turns open data into decisions players feel, building data literacy and showing why reserves, checklists, and listening to warnings matter. Safety in space comes from planning, not luck.
details:
What it does and how it works
The Human Margin is a five-chapter choice game for ages 7-12. The player is a first-person astronaut at an outpost on the rim of Shackleton Crater, with three crewmates and a little sister, Mimi, who asks questions on video calls. Each chapter is built on one NASA open dataset and one decision: a storm shelter (DONKI, NASA radiation limits), clean air and food (CO2 limits, OSDR Veggie experiments), a rover ice run (LRO), dust and power triage (Apollo records, DONKI), and a final launch budget. Every button shows its cost in Power, Air, Shield, Food or rover battery. Minigames (shelter drill, scrubber swap, route planner, power triage, launch checklist) make the numbers hands-on.

What makes it creative
Every risky choice is tied to a real spaceflight mistake, such as Apollo 12, Apollo 13, Gemini 8, Skylab 4 and Mir. A small tag previews the history, and a full History Echo card follows. Each hazard gives two warnings (a crewmate speaks, then an alarm) so the player has a chance to listen. In the last chapter, the storm forecast comes from the real Sun: the game pulls the strongest flare from the last 7 days through the DONKI API, with a September 2017 storm as an offline backup.

Benefits and impact
Children practice reading data, keeping reserves and listening to small warnings. Failure never feels like a punishment. Five gentle “Learning Endings” show what went wrong and end with a question for the player, and a Rewind button is always available. A Data Journal at the end links to the real datasets so curious players can keep exploring.

Tools
[Game engine and language], [art tools], NASA DONKI API via api.nasa.gov, and open data from OSDR, LRO/LROC and NASA OCHMO.

Factors we considered
Age-appropriate tone with nothing graphic, a small art budget (8 backgrounds, 14 sprites), and accuracy. The limits (250 mSv per storm, 600 mSv career, 3 mmHg CO2) are NASA’s. Cube counts and storm strengths are our design choices, and we say so.
